# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

response:
# Review: "Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem" (Varga & Holm comment)

The comment is right about most of the measurement problems, and several of them match points in my earlier review of the Halden paper:
- the per-hour metric guarantees "gains in every sector";
- manager-reported output is biased;
- the hours denominator assumes scheduled hours were worked;
- the revenue figure is nominal.

The attrition finding is new and important. If the microdata show that seven of the nine "preparation-phase" withdrawals happened after the schedule began, the working paper misdescribes its own sample. The Halden authors need to answer that directly.

The comment's **conclusion**, however, goes well beyond its evidence, and it treats its own sources inconsistently. The details follow.

## Arithmetic check

| Figure | Check | |
|---|---|---|
| 95.1 / 0.8 | +18.9% | ✓ |
| 98.4 / 0.859 | +14.6% | ✓ |
| 95.4 / 0.861 | +10.8% | ✓ |
| Hours 40.3 → 34.6 | −14.1%, ratio 0.859 | ✓ |
| Hours 40.4 → 34.8 | −13.9%, ratio 0.861 | ✓ |
| Real revenue 1.014 / 1.041 | −2.6% | ✓ |
| "Overstated reduction by roughly six points" | 20 − 14.1 = 5.9 | ✓ |
| 19 of 23 managers above records | Sign test p ≈ 0.003 (two-sided) | Systematic, as claimed |
| **Hours decomposition (§3)** | See below | ✗ |
| **Novelty extrapolation (§6)** | See below | ✗ |

**The hours components don't add up to the total.** Four scheduled days of 8 hours plus 0.7 hours each gives 34.8 hours. Adding 1.6 logged hours on the day off gives about 36.4. The reported total is 34.6, which is lower than the four-day figure alone. Either "+0.7 hours per day" is measured against a different base, or one of the figures is wrong. This needs fixing, because the decomposition is the evidence for *why* actual hours fell by less than scheduled hours.

**The novelty extrapolation gives the wrong month.** A straight line from 0.61 SD at month 3 to 0.29 SD at month 6 falls by about 0.107 SD per month. It reaches zero at about month 8.7, not "around month ten." This is minor in itself, but see §5 below on whether the extrapolation is meaningful at all.

## 1. The conclusion contradicts evidence the comment itself cites

The headline claim is that per-hour gains "reported for reduced-hours schemes" are "entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty."

That claim covers reduced-hours schemes generally, not just Halden. The comment cites the Varden trial approvingly, calling its counter-stratum result "the most reliable finding in the literature." Yet the same trial's case-processing stratum meets almost every standard the comment recommends:
- **Measurement:** output came from administrative records, and actual hours came from timesheets.
- **Selection:** offices were randomised, with no voluntary enrolment and no differential dropout.
- **Duration:** results ran to nine months.

That stratum found **+12.5% output per actual hour** (CI +6.9 to +18.4). This is not artifact of measurement or selection. At most it could be novelty, and nine months is longer than the period over which the comment's own extrapolation says enthusiasm returns to baseline.

The comment cannot use one Varden stratum as the best evidence and ignore the other. A defensible conclusion would be something like:

> "Halden's reported 23.4% gain is substantially overstated; corrected estimates in the subsets where correction is possible are around 11%. Whether residual gains are durable is unknown. The only randomised evidence finds real per-hour gains in backlog-driven work and output losses in coverage-bound work."

Note too that the comment's own best estimate, about 11% in the corrected subset, is close to Varden's randomised case-processing estimate.

## 2. The abstract says attrition was corrected; Table 2 doesn't correct it

The abstract says: "Correcting the first three [problems]... the gain falls... to 10.8%." The first three problems include attrition, but Table 2 corrects only output and hours. Attrition is never quantified, and it cannot be from survivor data alone. The abstract also says four problems "account for most of the reported gain." Revenue, the fourth, has no bearing on the per-hour estimate.

Attrition probably matters a great deal, so it deserves a number. Options include:
- bounds, such as Lee bounds or worst-case assumptions about the nine withdrawals;
- withdrawers' partial-period output, if the microdata contain any.

The comment also accounts for only eight of the nine exit reasons (six workload, two scheduling).

## 3. Table 2 compares different samples

Each row of Table 2 uses a different set of organisations: 61, 23, 27 and 17. The fall from 23.4% to 10.8% therefore mixes two things:
- the effect of the corrections;
- differences between the organisations in each subset.

If the 17 organisations with both records and time tracking had below-average reported gains to begin with, part of the apparent correction is just sample composition.

The fix is to compute all four specifications **within the same 17 organisations**, starting with their manager-reported output over scheduled hours. Only then does the table show what each correction contributes.

The data note acknowledges that the subsets are non-random. But the abstract and conclusion then generalise from them anyway.

## 4. Records are treated as ground truth

Billable hours, tickets closed and cases completed are better than a sponsor's rating. However, they capture single dimensions of output, may miss quality or changes in the mix of work, and also vary across organisations. The 3.8-point gap is good evidence that the manager index is biased upward. It doesn't establish that 95.1 is the true figure. One sentence saying so would make the argument stronger.

## 5. Novelty is asserted, not tested

**Energy is not output.** The comment infers that output gains are temporary from a two-point trend in self-reported energy. Even taken at face value, that shows enthusiasm fading, not productivity fading.

**A straight line through two points is not a forecast.** A rise followed by partial decline could just as easily level off above baseline.

**The direct test is available and unused.** The Halden output index was collected *monthly*, and the comment has the microdata. If the novelty account is right, output per hour should peak early and decline across months 1–6, which the comment can check directly. Reporting that trajectory, ideally for the 17 corrected organisations, would show whether output gains fade.

**The burden-of-proof argument changes the question.** That argument justifies saying durability is *unestablished*. It does not justify concluding that gains are "entirely" artifact.

## 6. The meetings section misdescribes the Varden analysis

- **"Selected for analysis after the results were known."** The calendar data were collected in month six of a nine-month trial, at managers' request. The seven offices are not a chosen subgroup; they are the *entire* treated arm of a pre-registered stratum.
- **"Suggest this as a mechanism... should not be cited as a mechanism."** The Varden authors explicitly said the analysis was unregistered, rested on seven offices, and "cannot establish a mechanism." They registered a confirmatory test. The comment is criticising a claim they did not make.
- **The standards of evidence are inconsistent.** The comment dismisses an n = 7 correlation while relying on n = 3 retail organisations (§5) and a two-point extrapolation (§6).
- **It undermines the comment's own thesis.** If meeting cuts do explain the per-hour gain, the gain is real: low-value time was removed. It would be a genuine productivity effect, not an artifact of measurement, selection or novelty.

The legitimate point is narrower: a seven-office correlation is weak evidence and should wait for the registered replication. That is the Varden authors' own position.

## 7. Smaller points

- **Retail.** "The three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%." Three organisations can't support a sectoral estimate. The match with Varden's −11.4% is a coincidence, since the two figures measure different things.
- **"Most reliable finding in the literature."** Varden's counter stratum has 5 offices per arm. As I noted in my review of Varden, its conventional clustered CIs are likely too narrow. Also, the negative result depends on how the trial was run: fixed headcount and unchanged opening hours make an output loss close to arithmetically certain.
- **Deflator.** CPI is a rough deflator for business revenue; sector output price indices would be better. The −2.6% real figure is still a fair correction to a misleading presentation.
- **Unlogged work.** "Some further work on the day off is probably not logged." The same is true of baseline work, so the bias in the change in hours is uncertain in direction.
- **The discrepancy with the working paper.** The microdata contradict the working paper's account of when the nine organisations withdrew. The comment should say whether the Halden authors were asked to explain this before publication.

## Overall

Sections 1–4 are a valuable correction and should stand, once the hours decomposition is fixed and the corrections are recomputed within a common sample. Sections 5–8 turn "the Halden estimate is inflated and its durability unknown" into "per-hour gains are entirely artifact." That claim needs evidence the comment doesn't present, and it is contradicted by the randomised study the comment itself relies on.

Suggested priorities:
1. Recompute Table 2 within the same 17 organisations.
2. Reconcile the hours decomposition.
3. Bound the effect of attrition.
4. Test novelty using the monthly output data.
5. Rewrite the conclusion so it covers Halden only and reflects Varden's case-processing result.

I can draft a revised Abstract and Conclusion along these lines if that would help.
